prompt: A rifle company commander has encrypted all company radio traffic and considers Electronic Protection complete. Which assessment best reflects the lesson?
options: Complete: encryption protects the signal, and the EW cell supplies any other measures
Incomplete: hopping and EMCON are applied only by the EW cell
Incomplete: EP needs several measures together, and every unit applies them
Complete: encryption protects both the content and the location of the radios
explanation: Slides 14 and 24 say encryption protects what is said but not jamming or location, and that EP means hard to find, jam and read through several measures together that every unit applies. The location option is the closest distractor, but Slide 14 states that encryption does not hide location.

prompt: Which list gives the five EP measures named in PAM 3-0702-01, paragraph 0110?
options: Hardening, encryption, frequency hopping, terrain masking, spectrum management
Radio discipline, encryption, frequency hopping, emission control, spectrum management
Hardening, encryption, frequency hopping, emission control, spectrum management
Hardening, encryption, frequency hopping, emission control, PACE planning
explanation: Slide 7 lists the five EP measures as hardening, encryption, frequency hopping, emission control and spectrum management. The terrain-masking list is the closest distractor, but terrain masking and radio discipline are field practices taught on Slides 9 and 10 and are not among the five named measures.

prompt: A student reads the example duel and concludes that fielding frequency hopping ends the contest. Which statement best corrects this?
options: Hopping ends the contest against spot jamming, so barrage jamming needs encryption
Hopping defeats jamming outright, so further measures only add emissions
The example shows ECM winning, since each of our measures is defeated
The enemy answers hopping with barrage jamming, so protection needs further layers
explanation: Slide 6 shows the enemy switching to barrage jamming after our radios hop, and our reply adding lower power, terrain masking and PACE: every move invites a counter-move. The encryption option is the closest distractor, but Slide 14 says encryption does not stop jamming.

prompt: A patrol must send a contact report while the enemy is known to be using direction finding. Which transmission best applies the radio-discipline rules?
options: A full, detailed message at the lowest power so that nothing has to be repeated
A short brevity-coded message at high power so it is received first time
A short brevity-coded message repeated at fixed intervals to confirm receipt
A pre-planned message in brevity codes, short, at the lowest power that works
explanation: Slide 9 asks for the lowest power that works, short pre-planned transmissions with brevity codes, and no fixed patterns. The high-power option is the closest distractor, but it breaks the power rule that limits the range of enemy DF.

prompt: Which pairing of enemy question and Electronic Protection answer is correct?
options: Can I FIND you? Encryption, brevity codes, and saying less, less often
Can I JAM you? Frequency hopping, directional antennas and PACE alternate means
Can I READ you? Emission control, low power, short transmissions and terrain masking
Can I JAM you? Emission control, low power and short transmissions
explanation: Slide 8 answers "Can I JAM you?" with frequency hopping, directional antennas and PACE alternate means. The last option is the closest distractor, but emission control, low power and short transmissions answer the "Can I FIND you?" question.

prompt: Two company positions must link by radio, with the enemy beyond a ridge to the east. Which antenna arrangement best applies the lesson?
options: A directional antenna aimed at the friendly station, placed on the ridge crest for a clear path
A directional antenna aimed at the friendly station, with a camouflage net across its front
A directional antenna aimed at the friendly station, at higher power to overcome the ridge
A directional antenna aimed at the friendly station, off the skyline with the ridge between it and the enemy
explanation: Slides 9 and 10 say to point the energy at your own station, keep antennas off skylines, and put terrain between the antenna and the enemy. The ridge-crest option is the closest distractor, but a crest sits on the skyline and removes the screening that the ridge would give.

prompt: A battalion command post kept transmitting from one unchanged site around the clock and was later struck. Which lesson from the Ukraine slide fits best?
options: DF leads to fires on emitters
Static emissions get hit
Blending works in busy networks
Mask first, move later
explanation: Slide 23 says command posts were high-payoff targets because their emissions were stationary and constant. DF leads to fires is the closest distractor, but that lesson concerns drone control stations located by direction finding and then engaged by indirect fire.

prompt: A command post has two usable sites: a hilltop with wide radio coverage, and the far side of a ridge from the enemy with weaker coverage. Enemy DF and jammers are active. Which decision follows the lesson?
options: Use the hilltop and add power to make up for the DF risk
Use the reverse slope; terrain between the antenna and the enemy blocks DF and jamming
Use the hilltop with a directional antenna and nets, since coverage outweighs the risk
Use the hilltop but vary report times so DF cannot establish a pattern
explanation: Slide 10 says to avoid hilltops for command posts because they are easy to DF and easy to jam, and to use the reverse slope. Varying report times is the closest distractor, but it applies a Slide 9 rule that does not remove the hilltop's exposure.

prompt: What lesson does the home-on-jam slide draw for our own emitters?
options: Any strong emitter, jammer or radio, can be located and struck
Jammers are at risk, but radios are protected by encryption
Emitters on a fixed frequency can be guided on, so hopping removes the risk
Air assets are at risk, but ground units face no such threat
explanation: Slide 22 draws the lesson that any strong emitter, jammer or radio, can be located and struck, and that our own EA teams face the same risk. The encryption option is the closest distractor, but Slide 14 says encryption protects content and does not hide location.

prompt: A brigade at the field baseline EMCON is told that attacks are under way and one system shows signs of compromise. Which decision follows the EMCON table?
options: Go to EMCON 4, RED, switching non-essential emitters off and using alternates
Stay at EMCON 3, AMBER, and set the compromised system to hop mode
Go to EMCON 5, BLACK, and isolate the compromised system
Go to EMCON 2, YELLOW, limiting transmissions and watching power levels
explanation: Slide 12 sets EMCON 5 BLACK for attacks under way, the most restrictive level, with compromised systems isolated. EMCON 4 RED is the closest distractor, but it applies after an attack has occurred and uses alternates instead of isolating compromised systems.

prompt: Which statement correctly matches an EMCON level with its condition?
options: EMCON 2, YELLOW: an attack has occurred
EMCON 4, RED: attacks are under way
EMCON 3, AMBER: a risk has been identified
EMCON 1, GREEN: a risk has been identified
explanation: Slide 12 pairs EMCON 3 AMBER with a risk identified, EMCON 2 YELLOW with a risk of attack, EMCON 4 RED with an attack that has occurred, and EMCON 5 BLACK with attacks under way. The EMCON 4 option is the closest distractor, but it swaps the condition for EMCON 5.

prompt: According to the EMCON slide, what should units do about changing between EMCON levels?
options: Rehearse moving between levels in every exercise
Hold the unit at the field baseline during exercises
Practise only the end levels, EMCON 1 and EMCON 5
Wait for a real attack before using the higher levels
explanation: Slide 12 says to rehearse moving between levels in every exercise and not just on paper. Practising only the end levels is the closest distractor, but it skips the intermediate steps that a unit actually has to move through.

prompt: Which statement correctly separates encryption from anti-jam measures?
options: Encryption keeps the link alive under attack; hopping and terrain protect what is said
Encryption protects what is said; anti-jam measures keep the link working
Encryption hides the transmitter's location; low power and masking stop jamming
Encryption and hopping do the same job, so a radio needs only one of them
explanation: Slide 14 says encryption protects WHAT you say, anti-jam protects WHETHER it gets through, and you need both. The first reversed option is the closest distractor, but it swaps the two jobs.

prompt: A platoon's radios are in secure mode on a fixed channel, and the net is jammed. Which statement best explains the failure and the fix?
options: Secure mode should already stop jamming, so check the encryption fill and reload it
Hop mode would expose the content, so keep a fixed channel and add a directional antenna
Secure mode protects content, not delivery; set the radios to HOP as well as SECURE
Secure mode shields the channel from jamming, so the likely cause is friendly interference
explanation: Slide 14 says the tactical radio gives both protections if it is set to HOP and SECURE, and that encryption does not stop jamming. The fill-reload option is the closest distractor, but it assumes encryption should resist jamming, which Slide 14 rules out.

prompt: Which statement correctly contrasts frequency hopping and spread spectrum?
options: Hopping spreads the signal over a wide band; spread spectrum jumps channels in a pattern only friendly radios know
Hopping jumps channels in a pattern only friendly radios know; spread spectrum spreads the signal
Both jump channels in a pattern only friendly radios know, but spread spectrum adds encryption
Hopping makes the signal harder to detect; spread spectrum makes it harder to read
explanation: Slide 13 says the hopping radio jumps channels many times per second in a pattern only friendly radios know, while spread spectrum spreads the signal so it is harder to detect and jam. The first swapped option is the closest distractor, but it reverses the two descriptions.

prompt: A signaller disconnects the antenna and the noise drops. After moving a short distance, the noise changes greatly. Which conclusion best fits both results?
options: The source is outside the radio, and terrain or direction is involved
The source is inside the radio, and terrain is not involved
The source is outside the radio, but terrain and direction are not involved
The source is the radio's power supply, and the antenna is faulty
explanation: Slide 15 says that noise dropping with the antenna disconnected means it comes from outside, and that a big change after moving or turning the antenna means terrain or direction is involved. The second option is the closest distractor, but it ignores the second result of the test.

prompt: According to the report slide, how is an interference report sent when the net is jammed?
options: On the jammed net once, in the clear, because the enemy already knows
On the jammed net in secure mode, because encryption stops jamming
Held until the jamming ends so the report is complete
Through the chain to the S6 and the EW cell, using an alternate means
explanation: Slide 17 says the report goes through the chain to the S6 and the EW cell, by an alternate means if the net is jammed, and never in the clear on the jammed net. Holding it until the jamming ends is the closest distractor, but Slide 16 calls for reporting during the event and the report feeds ES, the EOB and the commander's response.

prompt: Which pairing of interference-report line and content is correct?
options: FREQUENCY / NET: the affected frequency, net or system such as GPS
WHERE: the type of interference, such as noise, tones or false signals
EFFECT: what you did and the result
WHO: the date-time group the interference started
explanation: Slide 17 defines FREQUENCY / NET as the affected frequency, net or system, for example GPS. The WHERE option is the closest distractor, but WHERE holds your grid and the bearing to the source if known, while the type of interference belongs to WHAT.

prompt: A section drafts its PACE plan for a jamming exercise. Which draft reproduces the example plan in the lesson?
options: P: tactical radio, hop and secure; A: runner or visual signals; C: field wire or messenger vehicle; E: HF radio or another net
P: tactical radio, hop and secure; A: HF radio or another net; C: field wire or messenger vehicle; E: runner or visual signals
P: HF radio or another net; A: tactical radio, hop and secure; C: runner or visual signals; E: field wire or messenger vehicle
P: tactical radio, hop and secure; A: field wire or messenger vehicle; C: HF radio or another net; E: runner or visual signals
explanation: Slide 18 gives the example plan: tactical radio in hop and secure mode, then HF radio or another frequency or net, then field wire or messenger vehicle, then runner or visual and pyrotechnic signals. The last option is the closest distractor, but it swaps the alternate and contingency means.

prompt: A patrol's GPS gives a steady position that looks plausible, but the time is wrong and a speed shows while the patrol is stationary. Which interpretation and action best fit the lesson?
options: Suspect spoofing; cross-check with map, compass and terrain, and report it
Suspect jamming, because the fix is lost, and wait for the signal to return
Suspect a receiver fault, then reset it and trust the new fix
Suspect spoofing, but rely on the CRPA antenna to correct the position
explanation: Slide 19 says spoofing gives a wrong fix that looks right, lists wrong time and speed while stationary as red flags, and calls for cross-checks and reporting. The CRPA option is the closest distractor, but CRPA antennas null out jammers and do not correct a spoofed position.

prompt: A radar crew finds that jamming arrives from the side while the main antenna looks ahead. Which technique lets the radar ignore it?
options: Frequency agility, changing frequency pulse to pulse
Pulse compression, squeezing a coded pulse on receive
Low-probability-of-intercept waveforms, using low-power wideband signals
Sidelobe blanking, with a second antenna spotting the jamming
explanation: Slide 21 describes sidelobe blanking as a second antenna spotting jamming that arrives from the side, so the radar ignores it. Frequency agility is the closest distractor, but it changes frequency pulse to pulse and does not discriminate the direction of arrival.

prompt: Which pairing of radar technique and effect is correct?
options: Low-probability-of-intercept: low-power, wideband waveforms that are hard for ES to detect
Frequency agility: a second antenna spots jamming from the side and the radar ignores it
Sidelobe blanking: a long coded pulse is squeezed on receive for range detail
Pulse compression: the radar changes its frequency from one pulse to the next, like a hopping radio
explanation: Slide 21 describes low-probability-of-intercept as low-power, wideband waveforms that are hard for ES to detect. The pulse compression option is the closest distractor, but the radar changing frequency from pulse to pulse is frequency agility.
